summary: Describes the processcalendar extension to the Sieve email filtering language. It lets Sieve scripts process machine-readable calendar data carried inside email messages using MIME.

plainLanguage.summary: Email filter rules can now look at meeting invitations tucked inside messages and act on them, such as sorting them into the right place.

questions: how to filter calendar attachments in sieve
what is the sieve processcalendar extension
how does sieve process calendar invitations
what does the processcalendar action do
subtitle: A Sieve extension that lets mail filter scripts add, update or remove calendar events found inside incoming email.

tldr.problem: People get invitations, replies and cancellations for events by email, and it is useful to have the calendar data in those messages applied to their calendars automatically. Plain Sieve scripts had no way to do that.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds one action, processcalendar, which parses calendar data in a message and creates, updates or deletes calendar objects. Tagged arguments control which messages are trusted, where new items go, and how cancellations and results are handled.
tldr.outcome: Because the action changes a calendar without user interaction, the RFC sets strict rules and tells script writers to combine it with spam, sender and authentication checks.

today: RFC 9671 is a Proposed Standard from October 2024. It is not obsoleted and has no updates.

sections.title: Why Sieve Needs Calendar Processing
sections.content:
Users often receive invites, replies and cancellations for events and tasks as email. This RFC defines the processcalendar extension to the Sieve email filtering language (RFC 5228), so that a script can alter items on the user's calendars based on machine-readable calendar data carried in a message with MIME (RFC 2045).

Such messages are typically based on the iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol (iMIP, RFC 6047). But the enclosed iCalendar data may lack an iTIP method property, or may be in another format such as JSCalendar (RFC 8984). The extension is meant to work with any machine-readable calendar format that can express similar concepts. A Sieve interpreter that implements it must advertise the capability identifier processcalendar.
sections.plainLanguage: Meeting invites often arrive as email. This gives the mail sorter a new skill: reading the invite and updating your calendar.

sections.title: How the processcalendar Action Behaves
sections.content:
The processcalendar action parses the encapsulated calendar data and acts on its content. If the data is malformed in any way, it MUST be ignored and no action is taken. Otherwise calendar objects may be created, updated or deleted.

If a message holds calendar data in several MIME parts, the action MUST check that the parts are semantically equivalent. If they differ, it MUST NOT process the message; otherwise it processes only one representation.

The action MUST NOT change the recipient's participant status, which is out of scope. It SHOULD remove alarms from the data before applying it, because leaving them could trigger unwelcome notifications.

Some arguments depend on other Sieve extensions: :organizers needs extlists, and :outcome and :reason need variables. Using them without the extension is an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The sorter reads the invite. If it looks broken, it ignores it. It also never says yes or no to the meeting for you, and it switches off any beeping reminders that came attached.

sections.title: The Tagged Arguments
sections.content:
Several optional arguments shape the action:

  • :allowpublic lets the implementation process calendar data with no ATTENDEE properties, such as iTIP messages with METHOD PUBLISH. Without it, the data MUST be a well-formed iTIP message whose target matches one of the recipient's email addresses (the ORGANIZER for a REPLY, an ATTENDEE for REQUEST, CANCEL or ADD).
  • :addresses lists extra email addresses that belong to the recipient.
  • :updatesonly stops new objects being added; only existing ones are updated. :calendarid names the calendar that receives new objects, otherwise the implementation's default calendar is used. The two are incompatible, and using both is an error.
  • :deletecancelled says a cancellation SHOULD remove the object. Without it, the object is marked cancelled and stays.
  • :organizers names an external list of addresses whose events the recipient accepts. The ORGANIZER must match one of them.

The last two arguments, :outcome and :reason, each name a variable that receives the result.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules have switches: which senders to trust, which calendar to use, and whether a cancelled meeting is erased or just crossed out.

sections.title: Other Actions and Examples
sections.content:
The action does not cancel Sieve's implicit keep, so the message still lands in the mailbox. It can run only once per script; a script that tries two or more MUST fail with an error. It is incompatible with the reject and ereject actions.

The RFC's examples show an address list with a target calendar, processing airline itineraries with :allowpublic when the message comes from a specific sender and the subject contains a keyword, and recording the outcome and reason in headers with the editheader extension when nothing was added or updated.
sections.plainLanguage: The email stays in your inbox even after the calendar is updated, and the sorter only gets one go at calendar work per message.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
This extension alters a calendar without user interaction, so unless precautions are taken it can be a vector for calendar abuse. Implementations must follow the stated restrictions. The RFC says:

  • It MUST NOT process calendar data in a message flagged as spam or malicious (the spamtest and virustest extensions, RFC 5235, can help).
  • It SHOULD NOT process data from a potentially malicious or untrustworthy sender, and SHOULD only process data from a known sender. Allow and deny lists, signatures, SPF, DKIM and DMARC results can inform this.
  • For embedded attachments, implementations SHOULD decode and scan them, and MUST NOT process the data if an attachment is malicious.

On privacy, the RFC believes no considerations arise beyond those in RFC 5228.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting a robot write on your calendar is risky, so it should only trust mail that is not junk and comes from people or places you know.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has added the capability name processcalendar to the Sieve Extensions registry, with the contact address being the Sieve discussion list. It also added the action to the Sieve Actions registry defined by RFC 9122. The registration says the action does not cancel the implicit keep, cannot be used with IMAP events, and is incompatible with reject and ereject.
sections.plainLanguage: The new skill was written in the official list of mail filter skills so everyone can find it.

items.label: Nothing done
items.desc: No calendar data, or the options stopped processing.

items.label: Added
items.desc: A new calendar object was added.

items.label: Updated
items.desc: An object was updated, cancelled or removed.

items.label: Error
items.desc: Processing would have happened but failed.
